articles.title: How much will a solar panel charge your power station?
articles.summary: A solar panel rarely delivers the watts printed on it. This guide explains how panels make electricity, what raises and lowers their output, and how to work out what a day of sun puts into your battery.
articles.imageAlt: Two folding solar panels propped up to face the sun on a campsite lawn, wired to a portable power station in front of them.

sections.title: The short answer

blocks.text: On a typical day, a portable solar panel puts about three times its rated watts into a power station’s battery, counted in watt-hours. A 200 W panel returns roughly 630 Wh. That refills a 1,000 Wh power station in a little over a day and a half of ordinary sun.
The estimate is three numbers multiplied together: the watts on the panel’s label, the peak sun hours where you are, and the share of the panel’s output that actually reaches the battery.

blocks.text: The rest of this guide explains where each of those numbers comes from, so you can adjust them for your own panel, place and season. If you’d rather skip the math, [the calculator](/calculator/use-case) runs it for you and checks which panels each power station can take.

sections.title: How a solar panel makes electricity

blocks.text: A solar panel is a sheet of silicon cells with no moving parts. Sunlight arrives as particles called photons. When a photon with enough energy lands in a cell, it knocks an electron loose from the silicon.

Left alone, a loose electron would settle straight back. To prevent that, each cell is made of two layers of silicon treated in different ways, which creates a built-in electric field where they meet. The field pushes every freed electron the same way, toward the front of the cell. Metal contacts collect them, and once a cable joins the front of the cell to the back, the electrons flow through it as direct current (DC), the same kind of electricity a battery stores.
Three things follow from the way a cell works, and they explain most of what a panel does outdoors:

items: **Current follows light.** Each photon frees at most one electron, so the current a cell makes rises and falls almost in step with the light landing on it. Half the light, about half the current.

**Voltage is set by the silicon, not the sun.** One cell makes only about half a volt, in strong light or weak. Panels wire dozens of cells in a chain to add those up, which is why a folding panel puts out 20 to 50 V.
**Nothing is stored.** A panel makes power only while light is hitting it. The battery in the power station does the storing.

blocks.text: What efficiency means

Efficiency is the share of the sunlight landing on a panel that leaves it as electricity. Today’s panels convert about 20% to 25%. Some of the rest is reflected and most of it becomes heat, which is why a panel in full sun is hot to the touch.

Efficiency decides how big a panel is, not how much power it makes. Two panels rated 200 W produce the same power in the same sun. The more efficient one is simply smaller and lighter for those 200 W. Compare panels by their rated watts, and use efficiency to judge size and weight.

sections.title: What the watts on the label mean

blocks.text: A panel’s rated power, also written as peak watts or Pmax, is measured indoors under a lamp, in a fixed set of conditions called Standard Test Conditions:

items: Light at 1,000 watts per square meter, about the strength of direct sun at noon on a clear day.
Cells held at 77 °F (25 °C).
Light striking the panel square on.

blocks.text: Outdoors those three rarely happen together. Bright sun heats the cells well past 77 °F, the sun is square to the panel for only a moment, and haze, dust and cables each take a little. In good midday sun, expect a folding panel to show 70% to 85% of its rated watts. That is normal, and it is the reason the estimate above counts on 70% and not 100%.
The label carries a few more figures. You need them later, to check that a panel suits a power station.

blocks.caption: The figures on a solar panel’s label
rows: The most the panel makes in test conditions. Use it to estimate energy.
The highest voltage the panel reaches, with nothing connected. Use it for the safety check against a power station’s voltage limit.
The voltage the panel runs at while it is charging.
The highest current the panel can push. Use it to check a power station’s current limit.
How much power the panel loses for each degree its cells heat up. Closer to zero is better.

sections.title: When a panel produces power

blocks.text: A panel produces power whenever light reaches its cells, but the amount swings enormously through a day. Direct sunlight does nearly all the work. Early and late in the day the sun is low, its light crosses more air and strikes the panel at a slant, and output is a small fraction of the midday figure. Under solid cloud a panel still works on scattered daylight, at roughly 10% to 25% of its clear-day output. At night it makes nothing.
Peak sun hours

Because the sun’s strength changes all day, counting hours of daylight tells you little. The useful measure is peak sun hours: the whole day’s sunlight added up and expressed as hours of full-strength sun, at 1,000 watts per square meter. A day with 4.5 peak sun hours delivers the same energy as four and a half hours of perfect noon sun, even though the sun was up for twelve.
Peak sun hours depend on where you are and the time of year. These are the three levels the calculator uses:

sections.title: What changes a panel’s output

blocks.text: Six things decide how close a panel gets to the number on its label. They are listed roughly in order of how much they matter.
How strong the light is

Output tracks light almost one for one. Thin high cloud or haze trims it a little. A passing cloud can cut it by more than half within seconds, and solid overcast leaves 10% to 25%. This is the largest effect of all, and the one you can’t change. Plan for it: size the battery so a dull day doesn’t leave you short, and treat sunny-day figures as the good case.
The angle to the sun

A panel collects the most light when the sun’s rays hit it square on. Turn it away and the same panel catches a narrower slice of the beam. Pointed 30° off, it still collects about 87% of the direct light. At 45° that falls to 71%, and at 60° to half.

This is why a panel lying flat on the ground does well at midsummer noon and poorly on a winter morning. A folding panel should stand on its legs, tilted to face the sun, and be turned to follow it two or three times a day. A quick check: stand a pen upright on the panel’s surface. When the pen casts no shadow, the panel is aimed straight at the sun. A fixed panel can’t follow the sun, so in the US it is mounted facing south at a tilt close to the local latitude, which gives the best total over a year.
Shade

Shade costs far more than its size suggests. The cells in a panel are wired in a chain, and the current through a chain is set by its weakest cell. Cover one cell with a leaf, a tent line or the corner of a roof rack and it holds back every cell wired to it.

Panels contain bypass diodes that let current skip a shaded group of cells, so one shadow costs a section of the panel and not all of it. Even so, a hand-sized shadow can take a third or more of the output. Keep the whole panel in the sun, and check again as the sun moves: a shadow that wasn’t there at ten can be across the panel by two.
Heat

Solar cells lose voltage as they warm, so a hot panel makes less power than a cool one in the same light. The loss is about 0.3% to 0.5% of the rated power for every degree Celsius above 25 °C (77 °F). The datasheet lists it as the temperature coefficient of Pmax.

What matters is the temperature of the cells, not of the air. In full sun, cells run 35 to 55 °F (20 to 30 °C) hotter than the air around them. On a 90 °F day they reach about 140 °F, and the panel gives up roughly 10% to 15% of its power to heat alone. On a cold, clear day the same panel can match or beat the number on its label.

Heat is a loss you can reduce. Stand the panel up so air moves behind it, and don’t lay it on a hot car roof, dark rock or asphalt. The cold has one catch, covered further down: a cold panel’s voltage climbs, and that matters when you check it against a power station’s limit.
Dirt and glass

Dust, pollen and dried rain spots block a few percent of the light, and more after weeks without rain. A bird dropping or a stuck leaf is worse, because it acts like shade on the cells under it. Wipe the panel with water and a soft cloth.

Glass in front of the panel costs much more. A panel behind a window or a windshield receives light that has already been partly reflected and filtered, usually at a poor angle too. Put the panel outside.
Cables and conversion

Power is lost between the panel and the battery as well. Cables warm slightly as current passes through them, and long, thin cables lose the most. The power station’s solar charge controller converts the panel’s voltage to the battery’s at about 95% to 98%, and the battery stores 2% to 3% less than it is given.

Use the cable that came with the panel, and keep extension cables short and thick. One part of the chain works in your favor: most power stations have a maximum power point tracking (MPPT) controller, which keeps adjusting the load on the panel to draw the most power it can make in the light of that moment.

blocks.text: Added together, these are why about 70% of a portable panel’s rated output reaches the battery over a day. A fixed panel manages about 75%: it is aimed once, carefully, and wired with short cables.

sections.title: How to estimate what a panel will generate

blocks.text: With those numbers in hand, the estimate takes a minute.

items: **Find the rated watts.** They are on the panel’s label and usually in its name: a “220W” panel is rated 220 W. For several panels, add them up.
**Pick the peak sun hours** for your place and season: 2.5 for limited sun, 4.5 for an average day, 6 for strong sun.
**Multiply the two, then by the share that reaches the battery:** 0.7 for folding panels, 0.75 for fixed ones.

blocks.caption: Two 220 W folding panels in strong sun

rows.label: Peak sun hours in strong sun
Energy into the battery in a day

blocks.caption: Energy a portable panel returns in a day
blocks.note: Rated watts × peak sun hours (2.5, 4.5 and 6) × 70%. An overcast day returns about a quarter of a typical one.

blocks.text: Power at a given moment

The same share gives the power to expect while the sun is out. In full midday sun, about 70% of a portable panel’s rated watts reach the battery: 140 W from a 200 W panel, 280 W from a 400 W one. The power station’s screen shows this as its solar input. If yours reads much lower at noon on a clear day, look for shade, a poor angle or a hot panel before blaming the panel itself.

sections.title: How to estimate charging time

blocks.text: Charging time is the battery’s capacity divided by what the panels deliver. There are two useful versions of the sum.
Days of sun

Divide the power station’s capacity in watt-hours by the energy the panels return in a day. This is the honest figure for planning, because it already allows for the morning, the evening and every hour the sun is low.

blocks.caption: A 1,000 Wh power station and a 200 W folding panel

rows.label: Energy from the panel on an average day

blocks.text: Hours of full sun

For a quick figure, divide the capacity by the power that reaches the battery in full sun, which is the rated watts × 0.7. The same pair needs 1,000 Wh ÷ 140 W, a little over 7 hours of full midday sun. An average day holds only 4.5 such hours, which is why the recharge runs into a second day.

blocks.caption: Days of average sun to recharge a power station from empty
blocks.note: Capacity ÷ (panel watts × 4.5 peak sun hours × 70%), rounded up. Twice the panel halves the time, as long as the power station’s solar input can take it.

blocks.text: Three things stretch these figures in practice:

items: **The solar input has a ceiling.** A power station accepts only so many watts of solar. Panel beyond that limit adds nothing, so check the input’s maximum before you buy a second panel.
**Devices take their share first.** Anything running while the sun is out is fed from the panels before the battery is. With 140 W coming in and a 60 W load running, 80 W is left for charging.
**The last stretch is slower.** Charging eases off near the top, so the final few percent take longer than the sum suggests.

sections.title: Which panels suit your power station

blocks.text: Every solar panel makes DC power, but a power station’s solar input accepts it only inside set limits. They are printed beside the port and in the manual, and they look like this: 11–60 V, 15 A, 500 W max. Check a panel against them in this order.

items: **Voltage, the limit that can do damage.** The panel’s open-circuit voltage (Voc) must stay under the input’s maximum. Leave a margin, because voltage rises as cells get colder: about 10% above the label at freezing, and close to 20% at −4 °F. A panel that sits just under the limit on a warm afternoon can exceed it on a frosty morning.

**Voltage, the low end.** The panel’s operating voltage (Vmp) must reach the input’s minimum, even when the panel is hot and its voltage has dropped. Below the minimum the power station doesn’t charge at all.

**Current.** The panel’s short-circuit current (Isc) should be at or under the input’s maximum amps. Many power stations hold back any current above their limit, but rely on that only if the maker says so.

**Power.** Panel watts beyond the input’s maximum do no good: the input takes its limit and the rest goes unused. A little extra is still worth having. Panels seldom reach more than about 80% of their rated watts, so an array up to 125% of the input’s limit is put to full use.

**Connector.** Most panels end in MC4 plugs. Power stations use XT60, XT60i, Anderson or a round DC socket, so you need the adapter cable that joins the two. Panels sold by the power station’s maker usually include it.

blocks.text: Never connect panels whose combined open-circuit voltage could exceed the solar input’s maximum, even briefly. Over-voltage damage is permanent. When in doubt, work the sum for the coldest morning you expect.
Wiring more than one panel
Two or more panels can be joined in two ways, and the difference decides which limit you run into.

blocks.caption: Two panels of 21.5 V and 12.4 A each, joined both ways

blocks.text: Against an input rated 11–60 V and 15 A, the series pair fits: 43 V becomes about 48 V on a cold morning, still under 60 V, and 12.4 A is under 15 A. The parallel pair asks for 24.8 A, well over the limit. Series is the usual choice for power stations with a wide voltage range. Wire only identical panels together, since a mismatched panel drags the others down to its level.
How many watts of panel you need
To keep going day after day, the panels have to return what your devices use. Divide a day’s use by the peak sun hours, then by the 70% that reaches the battery.

blocks.caption: Devices that use 900 Wh a day, in average sun

rows.label: Peak sun hours on an average day

blocks.text: Round up to what is sold, here 300 W, and check that total against the solar input’s limits. If the input can’t take enough panel to keep up, the battery has to be big enough to cover the shortfall, or you need a power station with a larger solar input.

[The calculator](/calculator/use-case) does all of this for you. Choose solar in the recharge step, and each power station is paired with panels its solar input can take, checked for voltage in the cold, current and power, with the wiring spelled out.

sections.title: Getting the most from your panels

items: Aim the panel at the sun, and turn it two or three times a day.
Keep every cell out of shade, and check again as the sun moves.
Stand the panel up so air can cool its back.
Wipe off dust, pollen and droppings.
Use short, thick cables, and put the panel outside, never behind glass.
Start early. The hours either side of noon carry most of a day’s energy, so a panel set up at ten catches far more than one set up at two.
Plan for a dull day. Size the battery to last without sun, and treat solar as what stretches it.

articles.title: How to Choose a Portable Power Station: The Complete Buying Guide
articles.summary: Three numbers decide which power station fits: how much energy it stores, how much power it delivers at once, and how hard it can push while a motor starts. This guide shows how to work out all three for your own devices, then how to judge the battery, the charging and everything else on the spec sheet.
articles.imageAlt: A gray portable power station on a living-room floor beside a dark armchair and a floor lamp, plugged into a wall outlet to charge.

sections.title: The short answer

blocks.text: Choose a power station by three numbers, in this order. **Capacity**, in watt-hours (Wh), decides how long it runs. **Continuous output**, in watts (W), decides what it can run at once. **Surge output** decides whether a refrigerator or a power tool will start at all. Get those right for your own devices first. Battery type, charging speed, weight and price come after.

For capacity, add up the watt-hours your devices use over the time you need power, then multiply by 1.5. That covers what is lost on the way out of the battery and leaves a reserve. For output, add up the watts of everything that runs at the same time and add a quarter.

blocks.caption: A refrigerator, Wi-Fi router, CPAP, lights and a phone through a 24-hour outage

rows.label: Energy the devices use in 24 hours
Losses and reserve, as a quick rule

blocks.text: On the AC outlets the same devices draw 212 W together, so they need about 270 W of continuous output, and about 900 W for the moment the refrigerator’s compressor starts. A power station of about 3,000 Wh covers all three with room to spare.

The rest of this guide explains each number and every other line on a spec sheet. If you’d rather skip the sums, [the calculator](/calculator/use-case) runs them on your own devices and hours and lists the power stations that fit.

sections.title: What a portable power station is

blocks.text: A portable power station is a rechargeable battery in a case with everything needed to use it: an inverter that turns the battery’s direct current (DC) into the alternating current (AC) of a wall outlet, USB and 12 V ports that skip the inverter, a charger, and a battery management system that guards the cells. You fill it from a wall outlet, solar panels, a car or a generator, and it gives the energy back later.

It burns no fuel, so it makes no exhaust and runs indoors, in a tent or in a closed van. That is its main advantage over a gas generator, which has to stay outside. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission counts nearly 100 deaths a year from the carbon monoxide of portable generators, and asks for at least 20 feet between a running generator and the house.

blocks.caption: A power station next to the alternatives
rows: Phones, tablets and laptops over USB. The only kind allowed on a plane
Small. Flight rules cap it at 100 Wh, and it rarely has an AC outlet
Appliances, tools and electronics for hours or days, indoors or out
Stores energy but doesn’t make it. Once empty, it needs a source to refill it
Days of high power, for as long as the fuel lasts
Outdoors only, loud, and needs fuel and upkeep
Whole-house backup, wired into the electrical panel
Fixed in place, installed by an electrician, and far more expensive

blocks.text: There is a ceiling. Past about 8,000 Wh of capacity or 7,200 W of output, a plan has outgrown what a single portable unit is built for. That is the territory of stacked expansion batteries, a home battery or a generator.

sections.title: Capacity: how long it runs

blocks.text: Capacity is the energy the battery stores, in watt-hours. One watt-hour runs a one-watt device for an hour, so a 60 W laptop uses 60 Wh for every hour it is on. Watts are the rate and watt-hours are the amount. Small units are sometimes sold by milliamp-hours (mAh), a figure that means little without the voltage. Always compare watt-hours.
Work out what your devices use

items: **List the devices** you want to run and find the watts of each. The figure is on the label or the power adapter. If the label gives only amps, multiply by the voltage: 1.5 A at 120 V is 180 W.
**Multiply by the hours** each one runs during the time you need power.

**Allow for cycling.** A refrigerator’s compressor runs about 35% of the time, so a 150 W refrigerator uses 150 W × 24 h × 35% = 1,260 Wh a day, not 3,600 Wh. Heaters and air conditioners on a thermostat cycle the same way.
**Add everything up.**

blocks.caption: A day of outage essentials
blocks.note: Total: 1,948 Wh in 24 hours. These are the values the calculator starts from. Check the labels on your own devices.

blocks.text: From what the devices use to the capacity on the label
A battery never hands over everything printed on its label. Four things sit between the rated capacity and your devices:

items: **Conversion losses.** The inverter delivers about 92% of what it takes from the battery to an AC device. The USB and 12 V ports do slightly better, about 93%.

**The inverter’s own draw.** While the AC outlets are switched on, the inverter uses power even with nothing plugged in: about 5 W on a small unit and 20 to 40 W on a large one. Over a day that is 120 Wh to nearly 1,000 Wh.
**The part you can’t draw.** The battery management system keeps a little back at the bottom to protect the cells. About 95% of the rated capacity is usable.
**A reserve.** Batteries fade with age, estimates are never exact, and running to empty is hard on the cells. Keep 20% in hand.

blocks.caption: What the battery has to supply for the same day

rows.label: The inverter’s own draw, 5 W for 24 hours

blocks.caption: The rated capacity that supplies it

rows.label: Usable share of the rated capacity

blocks.text: Round up to the next size sold, here about 3,000 Wh. The quick rule from the top of this guide, multiplying by 1.5, lands within a few percent of the full sum.
How long a given capacity lasts
Turned around, the same numbers give runtime: the rated capacity × 95% × 92%, divided by the watts the device draws. A 1,000 Wh power station runs a steady 100 W load for roughly 8 hours.

blocks.caption: How long 1,000 Wh runs one device
blocks.note: Rated capacity × 95%, divided by the device’s watts ÷ 92% plus the inverter’s own draw of 5 W or more. Your devices will differ, so check their labels.

blocks.text: Cold shrinks a battery

A lithium battery gives back less in the cold: about 90% of its rated capacity between 32 and 50 °F, and about 80% below freezing. Most units also refuse to charge below 32 °F, to protect the cells. If you will use the power station in winter, size up, and keep it somewhere warmer when you can.

sections.title: Output: what it can run at once

blocks.text: Output is the power the inverter can deliver, in watts. Spec sheets give two figures. Continuous output, also called rated or running output, is what the unit holds for as long as the battery lasts. Surge or peak output is what it holds for a moment.
Continuous output

Add up the running watts of every AC device that will be on at the same time. Then leave headroom. Loads that run for hours should stay at or under 80% of the inverter’s rating, the rule electricians apply to continuous circuits, so multiply their total by 1.25. Brief loads such as a kettle or a saw can run closer to the limit: 10% on top of the highest total is enough for them.
Devices on the USB and 12 V ports don’t count toward this number. Those ports have converters of their own.

The outage essentials above draw 212 W on the AC outlets, which asks for about 270 W of continuous output. Any power station manages that. Add a microwave and a coffee maker to the same kitchen, used one at a time, and the picture changes: 212 W plus the 1,100 W microwave is 1,312 W, and with 10% on top the inverter needs about 1,450 W. One short-use appliance, not the refrigerator, decides the size of the inverter.
Running big appliances one at a time, not together, is the cheapest way to get by with a smaller unit.
Surge output

Motors and compressors draw two to five times their running power for a split second as they start. If the surge rating can’t cover that moment, the inverter shuts off, even though the running load is small.

blocks.caption: Running and starting watts of common appliances
blocks.note: Typical values, the ones the calculator starts from. The label or manual of your own appliance is the better source.

blocks.text: To check surge, take everything that is already running and add the largest single extra starting draw, since motors rarely start at the same instant. Then add 10%, because starting figures are estimates.

blocks.caption: Outage essentials at the moment the refrigerator starts

rows.label: Everything running on the AC outlets
Extra draw as the refrigerator starts, 750 W − 150 W

blocks.text: Boost modes are not extra output

Many units advertise a second, higher figure under names such as X-Boost or Power Lifting. In that mode the inverter lowers its voltage so that a heating appliance rated above the limit keeps running, more slowly. It suits simple heating appliances such as kettles and heaters. Electronics and many motors need full voltage, and it is not a higher continuous rating. Choose by the rated output.
Outlets and 240 V

Check the outlets as well as the watts. A standard 15 A outlet carries 1,800 W and a 20 A outlet 2,400 W, whatever the inverter behind it can do. To draw more than that through one cord, for an RV or a transfer switch, the unit needs a 30 A outlet.

Most portable units put out 120 V only. Dryers, ranges, central air conditioning and many well pumps need 240 V, which only some of the largest units supply, alone or as a linked pair. A single appliance that draws more than about 3,600 W is a sign you are past what a portable unit should run.

Every unit worth buying has a pure sine wave inverter, which makes the same smooth waveform as the grid. Avoid anything described as modified sine wave: motors run hot on it and some electronics refuse to work.

sections.title: The battery: chemistry and lifespan

blocks.text: The cells inside decide how long the power station lasts, how much it weighs and how it copes with cold. In 2026 nearly every new model uses lithium iron phosphate, written LFP or LiFePO4.

blocks.caption: Battery types in power stations sold in 2026
columns: Full cycles before it fades to 80%
rows: Nearly all current models, at every size
Lithium NMC, often sold as plain “lithium-ion”
Lighter by a third or more
Older models and a few small, light ones
Over 4,000, by the first maker’s figure
One first model, built for the cold
blocks.note: Cycle and weight figures are makers’ published specifications. One cycle is a full discharge and recharge.

blocks.text: What cycle life means for you

A cycle rating says how many times the battery can be fully drained and refilled before it holds 80% of what it did when new. It still works after that, with less capacity. At one full cycle every day, 3,000 cycles last more than 8 years and 6,000 last 16. Used a few times a month for camping or outages, an LFP battery won’t run out of cycles in any time you would notice.
Read the fine print on that rating. Some makers count cycles to 80% of the original capacity, some to 70% and some to 50%, and the lower the bar, the bigger the number looks. Compare like with like.

NMC still has one thing in its favor: weight. A 288 Wh NMC unit in our catalog weighs 5 lb, where LFP units of the same capacity weigh about 8 lb. If you carry the power station on foot and use it now and then, that can be the right trade. For anything used often, or kept for years against outages, choose LFP.
Sodium-ion and solid-state

Sodium-ion is the newest option. The first widely sold sodium-ion power station, a 900 Wh, 1,500 W unit from BLUETTI, launched in September 2025. Its maker says it charges down to 5 °F and runs down to −13 °F, temperatures at which most LFP units refuse to charge. The price is weight: 35 lb for 900 Wh, against about 25 lb for an LFP unit of 1,000 Wh. It makes sense if you work or camp in real cold. Otherwise LFP remains the better buy.

A few brands now label units “solid-state” or “semi-solid-state” and promise more energy for the weight. The claims may hold, but in 2026 the products are new, the only figures are their makers’ own, and long-term results don’t exist yet. Treat them as early.
Looking after the battery

items: Keep it at room temperature when it isn’t in use, not in a hot car or a freezing shed.
For long storage, leave it part-charged, between about half and 80%, and check it every three months, since the electronics drain it slowly. The manual gives the exact level the maker wants.
For outage duty, most units can stay plugged in and hold a charge limit you set in the app.

sections.title: Recharging: wall, solar, car and generator

blocks.text: How you will refill the battery matters as much as its size. A power station you can recharge every day can be much smaller than one that has to carry a whole trip or a whole outage on a single charge.
From a wall outlet

This is the fastest and simplest way. A household outlet supplies up to 1,800 W, and many current units use most of it: 1,000 Wh models now commonly refill in about an hour. To estimate the time for any unit, divide the capacity by the charging watts, then allow for the charger’s losses, about 10%, and for the slower last stretch, another 10%.

blocks.caption: Hours to recharge from empty at a wall outlet
blocks.note: Capacity ÷ (input watts × 90%) × 1.1. The input watts are on the spec sheet as AC input or AC charging power. A standard household outlet can’t supply more than 1,800 W.

blocks.text: Fast charging is useful between outages or on a short generator run, but it makes the fans loud. Many units let you turn the charging speed down in the app for a quiet overnight charge.
From solar panels

Solar is what makes a power station last for days. The number to check is the solar input: its maximum watts and the voltage range it accepts. Small units take about 100 W of panel, mid-size ones about 500 W, and the largest 2,400 W or more.

A portable panel puts about three times its rated watts into the battery on an average day, counted in watt-hours: 630 Wh from a 200 W panel. It takes about 500 W of panel to keep a refrigerator going day after day. Our guide to [how much a solar panel will charge your power station](/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station) has the full method, including the voltage check that keeps a panel from damaging the input.
From a car

A car’s 12 V socket is the slow way. It gives about 100 W, so 1,000 Wh takes ten hours of driving or more. It is fine for topping up a small unit and no way to refill a large one. Makers also sell alternator chargers that wire to the car’s battery and deliver 500 to 800 W while the engine runs.

An electric car with a household outlet, often called vehicle-to-load or V2L, is a different matter. The power station charges from it as it would from a wall outlet. The calculator lists the cars whose makers confirm such an outlet and checks each power station against it.
From a generator

A power station and a generator work well together: the generator runs for an hour or two, and the battery carries the quiet hours. The generator has to give clean power, which in practice means an inverter generator. The power station then charges at the lowest of three limits: what its own input takes, what the generator’s outlet carries, and 80% of the generator’s running watts.
Charging while in use
Most units can charge and power devices at the same time, called pass-through. Devices take their share first: with 300 W of solar coming in and a 200 W load running, 100 W is left for the battery.

sections.title: Ports and outlets

blocks.text: Count the things you will plug in at once, and match each one to a port.

items: **AC outlets.** Count them, check their type (15 A, 20 A or 30 A), and make sure bulky plugs and adapters won’t block the outlet beside them.
**USB-C.** A port rated 100 W or more charges a laptop directly, with no power brick and no inverter. Some new units go to 140 W.
**USB-A.** For older cables and small gadgets.
**12 V car socket.** Runs a 12 V refrigerator, a tire inflator or anything else with a car plug, usually up to about 120 W.
**Display and app.** A screen that shows watts in, watts out and time remaining is worth having. An app adds charge limits, charging speed and remote on and off.

blocks.text: Use the DC ports when you can

Every watt-hour that leaves through an AC outlet passes through the inverter, which loses about 8% and uses power of its own for as long as it is switched on. A laptop on USB-C or a refrigerator on the 12 V socket avoids both. In a camping setup with a 12 V refrigerator, lights and a phone, almost nothing needs the inverter, and a whole weekend fits in about 1,500 Wh.
Switch the AC outlets off when nothing is using them.

sections.title: Home backup: UPS, expansion and connecting to the house

blocks.text: Plan for the outage you fear, not the average one. Leaving out major storms, the average US customer loses power for about two hours a year. In 2024, three hurricanes pushed the average to 11 hours, the most in ten years, and the people in their paths were out for days.

The refrigerator sets the clock. Food in a closed refrigerator stays safe for about 4 hours without power, and a full freezer holds for about 48 hours. So a backup plan has to get the refrigerator running within a few hours and keep it going: about 630 Wh of capacity for an 8-hour outage, and 1,900 Wh for a full day.
UPS mode

With the power station plugged into the wall and a device plugged into it, most units pass grid power straight through and switch to the battery when the grid fails. The switch takes a moment. Makers quote 10 to 20 ms for current models, quick enough that lights, a router or a refrigerator never notice.

Sensitive electronics are less forgiving. A desktop computer or a network drive can restart if the gap is longer than its power supply can bridge. In one independent test of six power stations in 2023, the measured gap ran from 9 to 39 ms, and two units were slower than their makers claimed. If a computer has to stay up, test it: plug it in, pull the power station’s wall plug, and watch. For medical equipment that must never drop out, ask the equipment’s maker which backup it approves.
Expansion batteries

Many large units accept extra battery packs, which add capacity without adding output. That lets you buy for today’s need and grow later: one 2,765 Wh model in our catalog expands to more than 19,000 Wh. Check the price of the extra batteries before you commit, because they work only with their own maker’s units.
Connecting to the house

The simple way to use a power station in an outage is with extension cords: plug the refrigerator and the other essentials straight into it. To power circuits in the house instead, an electrician installs a transfer switch or an interlock with an inlet, and the power station connects to the inlet with a single cord, usually from its 30 A outlet.

Never plug a power station into a wall outlet to feed the house. Power sent back through the wiring can reach the utility lines and injure the people repairing them, and it can destroy the unit when the grid returns. A transfer switch or interlock, installed by an electrician, is the only safe connection.

sections.title: Weight, size and where it will live

blocks.text: Capacity is heavy. Current LFP models weigh 20 to 30 lb for every 1,000 Wh, so a choice of capacity is also a choice of weight.

blocks.caption: What LFP power stations weigh in 2026
rows: One hand, like a small toolbox
Wheels and a handle, and two people for stairs
blocks.note: Weights of models on sale in 2026, from their makers’ specifications.

blocks.text: Be honest about how far you will carry it. About 25 to 30 lb is comfortable in one hand from the car to a campsite. Past 60 lb, plan on wheels, a cart or a second person, and decide where the unit will live, because it won’t move often.
Weather

Most power stations are indoor appliances with no protection against water or dust. If the unit will sit outside, look for an IP rating on the spec sheet. Without one, keep it under cover, off wet ground and out of blowing dust. Heat matters too: cells age faster when hot, so give the unit shade and moving air, and don’t leave it in a closed car in summer.
Flying

A power station can’t go on a passenger flight. Airline rules limit lithium-ion batteries to 100 Wh each, or 160 Wh with the airline’s approval, and almost every power station is larger than that. For a trip by air, take a power bank of 100 Wh or less in your carry-on bag.

sections.title: Safety, certification and warranty

blocks.text: A power station is a large battery kept in your home, so who made it and how it was tested matter more than any feature.

items: **Look for a safety listing.** In the US and Canada the standard for these products is UL 2743, for portable power packs. The listing should come from a recognized test lab such as UL, ETL, CSA or TÜV, and it should cover the whole unit, not only the cells.

**Check for recalls.** Search the model on the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s site before you buy, and now and then afterward. In August 2026, Goal Zero recalled about 46,200 Yeti 3000X power stations because a circuit board could overheat. The fix was a free firmware update. Register your unit so the maker can reach you.

**Read the warranty.** Three years is the floor for a small unit and five years is normal for a large one. Check who handles claims in your country, and whether you have to register to get the full term.
**Buy from a maker that will be there.** Extra batteries, replacement cables and firmware updates all come from the maker. An unbranded unit at a low price has none of that behind it.

**Recycle it at the end.** Lithium batteries must not go in household trash or recycling bins, where they can start fires. Take the unit to an electronics recycler or a household hazardous waste site.

sections.title: What it should cost

blocks.text: Compare prices by the watt-hour: divide the price by the capacity. A 2,000 Wh unit at $1,000 costs 50¢ per watt-hour. In late 2026, LFP units from established brands run from about 40¢ to 70¢ per watt-hour. Small units cost more per watt-hour than large ones, and list prices are often cut by a fifth or more in sales, so it pays to watch a model for a few weeks.

Beyond capacity, you pay for a bigger inverter, faster charging, a larger solar input, expandability and a longer warranty. Pay for the ones your plan needs and skip the rest. An inverter far larger than your loads costs money, weight and idle power.
Bundles with solar panels or extra batteries can save money, but only if the panels suit the unit and you would have bought them anyway. Price the pieces separately first.
No federal tax credit in 2026

Until the end of 2025, a battery of 3 kWh or more could earn a 30% federal tax credit, and sellers of large power stations advertised it. That credit is not available for anything placed in service after December 31, 2025. If a listing still mentions it, the listing is out of date.

sections.title: What common setups need

blocks.text: These are worked with the calculator’s default devices, in mild weather, on one full charge with nothing recharging the battery.

blocks.caption: Capacity and output for six common setups
rows: Camping weekend: 12 V refrigerator, lights, phone
Remote workday: laptop, monitor, Starlink, router, phone
Job site: circular saw, drill, work light, tool battery charger
Outage essentials: refrigerator, router, lights, phone, CPAP
blocks.note: The two refrigerator setups also need about 830 to 900 W of surge output for the compressor’s start, and the job site 2,850 W for the saw. On the camping weekend almost everything runs from the DC ports, which is why the AC output is so small.

blocks.text: Two patterns stand out. Long, steady loads, a refrigerator or a satellite dish, drive capacity. Short, heavy ones, a saw or a microwave, drive output. Few setups are heavy on both, which is why a unit chosen for its capacity usually has more inverter than it needs.
[The calculator](/calculator/use-case) does this for your own list, adds cold weather and recharging, and shows which power stations fit.

sections.title: What is different in 2026

items: **LFP is the default.** A long-life battery no longer costs extra, and a 1,000 Wh unit now weighs about 25 lb and recharges in about an hour.
**Sodium-ion has arrived**, for people who need to charge below freezing.
**“Solid-state” labels are appearing** before the evidence for them.
**The federal tax credit is gone** for batteries placed in service after December 31, 2025.
**Recalls reach well-known brands.** Check the model before you buy, new or used.

sections.title: A checklist before you buy

items: **Capacity** covers your devices for the time you need, with losses and a 20% reserve: about 1.5 times what the devices use.
**Continuous output** is at least 1.25 times what runs for hours, and covers your largest short-use appliance on top.
**Surge output** covers everything running plus the biggest motor’s start.
**The battery** is LFP, with its cycle rating stated to 80% capacity.
**The charging inputs** match how you will refill it: AC watts for the wall, solar watts and voltage for panels.
**The ports and outlets** fit your devices, including a 30 A outlet if it will feed an RV or a transfer switch.
**The weight** is one you can lift, or the unit has wheels.
**The unit** carries a UL 2743 listing, has no open recall, and comes with a warranty of three to five years that is honored where you live.
**The price** per watt-hour is in line with similar units.

articles.title: How to Install a Solar Panel for the Most Power: Direction, Tilt and Shade
articles.summary: Which way a panel faces, how steeply it leans and what shades it decide how much sunlight it turns into power, and the right answers depend on where you are. Pick your spot on the map for its direction, tilt and sun path, then see what matters and what barely does.
articles.imageAlt: A row of black solar panels on a tilted ground mount in a backyard, angled up toward the sun, with tall pine trees behind it.

sections.title: The short answer

blocks.text: Face the panel toward the equator: south if you live north of it, north if you live south of it. Tilt it up from flat by a little less than your latitude. Then keep all of it out of shade from mid-morning to mid-afternoon. Those three choices decide most of what a panel collects; everything else is worth a few percent.

The three aren’t equal. Shade on a corner of the panel can cost a third of its output. Facing east or west instead of toward the equator costs a fifth to a quarter. A tilt a few degrees off costs almost nothing. The planner below works out the direction and tilt for your location, and the rest of this guide explains where its numbers come from.

sections.title: Find the direction and tilt for your location

blocks.text: Tap the map where the panel will go, or let your browser share your location. The planner shows which way to face the panel, how far to tilt it, and what a magnetic compass reads when it points the right way. Step through the months to see how high the noon sun climbs, how long the day is and where the sun rises and sets; the lines on the map follow along. The recommendations at the bottom change with your latitude.

zones.name: Near the equator
zones.summary: The noon sun is never far from overhead, so a panel works almost flat and its direction hardly matters. Heat and rain do more to its output than its angle.

zones.name: In the tropics
zones.summary: The sun passes straight overhead twice a year. For weeks around {midsummer} the noon sun stands on the {toPole} side of the sky, behind a panel that faces {toEquator}.

zones.name: In the subtropics
zones.summary: The noon sun climbs almost overhead in summer and stays well up in winter. Tilting starts to pay here: a flat panel gives up 8% to 14% of the year’s output.

zones.name: In the mid-latitudes
zones.summary: The noon sun’s height swings by nearly 47° between {midsummer} and {midwinter}, so the season matters as much as the place. A well-tilted panel collects about a fifth more than a flat one.

zones.name: In the high latitudes
zones.summary: Summer days are long and winter days short and low, so most of a year’s energy arrives between spring and autumn. Near 56°, a well-placed panel makes about a fifth as much in {midwinter} as in {midsummer}.

zones.name: Near the polar circle
zones.summary: The {midwinter} sun barely clears the horizon, while around {midsummer} it sets for only a few hours. At Anchorage (61° N), a well-placed panel made about a tenth as much in December as in May.

zones.name: Inside the polar circle
zones.summary: The sun stays down for part of winter and up day and night for part of summer. At Tromsø (69.6° N), a fixed panel made 94% of its year’s energy between March and September, and nothing at all in December and January.

recommendations.title: Face north, not south
recommendations.text: Most solar advice is written for the Northern Hemisphere. Below the equator panels face north: at Sydney, a panel tilted 30° toward the south collected 55% of what one facing north did.

recommendations.title: Don’t count on solar in {midwinter}
recommendations.text: For weeks around {midwinter} the sun doesn’t rise at all. A power station needs another way to recharge in that season, such as a wall outlet or a generator.

recommendations.title: Keep the whole panel in sun
recommendations.text: Shade on even a small part of a panel holds back the cells wired to it. Pick a spot that stays clear from mid-morning to mid-afternoon.

recommendations.title: Keep the whole panel in sun
recommendations.text: Shade on even a small part of a panel holds back the cells wired to it. Pick a spot that stays clear from mid-morning to mid-afternoon, and check it again around {midwinter}, when the noon sun is lowest and shadows are longest.

recommendations.title: Low sun means long shadows
recommendations.text: With the sun this low, a small rise or a shed throws a long shadow. Put the panel where it has a clear view of the horizon to the {toEquator}.

recommendations.title: Tilt it 10°, whichever way is easiest
recommendations.text: Nearly flat collects the most here, and at 10° rain still rinses the glass. In Singapore a panel at 10° made the same energy facing north, south or west, to within 1%, so face it wherever the shade is least.

recommendations.title: Tilt matters most here
recommendations.text: At Anchorage a flat panel collected 73% of what a well-tilted one did. Use the planner’s figure, or go steeper if you get snow.

recommendations.title: Set a fixed panel steep
recommendations.text: The sun is low all year, so steep angles work best. At Tromsø the best all-year angle was 49°, and a vertical panel facing {toEquator} still collected 79% of that while shedding snow.

recommendations.title: Watch which side the noon sun is on
recommendations.text: For weeks around {midsummer} the noon sun stands to the {toPole}. A fixed panel facing {toEquator} loses a little then; turn a portable one to face {toPole} at midday. Step through the months above to see when.

recommendations.title: Let air reach the back of the panel
recommendations.text: Heat is the biggest loss you control here. In full sun the cells run 20 to 30 °C above the air and give up 10% to 15% of their power on a hot day. Leave a gap behind a mounted panel, and stand a portable one on its legs rather than on sand, rock or a car roof.

recommendations.title: Portable panels: flat at midday, steep at the ends of the day
recommendations.text: Around noon the sun is close to overhead all year, so lay the panel nearly flat. In the early morning and late afternoon, tilt it steeply toward the east, then the west.

recommendations.title: Portable panels: turn it two or three times a day
recommendations.text: Face the morning sun, then {toEquator} around midday, then the afternoon sun. Each time, stand a pen upright on the panel: no shadow means it faces the sun squarely. That collects nearly as much as tracking the sun exactly.

recommendations.title: Portable panels: catch the summer mornings and evenings
recommendations.text: From spring to autumn the sun rises in the {toPole}east and sets in the {toPole}west, behind a panel that faces {toEquator}. Turning a portable panel toward it early and late pays more here than nearer the equator.

recommendations.title: Portable panels: follow the midnight sun
recommendations.text: When the sun stays up all night it circles the whole horizon, low in the {toPole} around midnight. Turn a portable panel to follow it, and stand it almost upright.

recommendations.title: Fixed mounts: change the angle twice a year
recommendations.text: If the mount adjusts, flatten the panel for {summerHalf} and steepen it for {winterHalf}. In Kansas City, 15° and 55° collected 4.7% more than the best single angle.

recommendations.title: If you get snow, lean steeper
recommendations.text: Snow slides off a steep panel sooner, and a panel under snow makes almost nothing. Going 8° steeper than the planner’s figure costs about 1% of a year’s output, or less.

recommendations.title: Plan on little from solar in {midwinter}
recommendations.text: Short, low days leave a panel with a small share of its summer output. Size the battery to get through winter without the sun, and treat solar as what stretches it.

blocks.text: The all-year tilt is the fit Jacobson and Jadhav published from the best fixed angles in every country. The compass reading comes from the World Magnetic Model, and the rest is the geometry of the sun, worked out for the 15th of the month. Your location is used in your browser and isn’t sent to Watt48.

sections.title: Why the angle matters

blocks.text: A panel collects the most when sunlight hits it square on. Light arriving at a slant spreads over more of the panel, so each cell gets less: 30° off square, a panel catches 87% of the direct beam, and 60° off, only half. The [guide to solar charging](/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station) covers the other things that cut a panel’s output.

Where square on points depends on the sun’s path. The sun crosses the sky from east to west and is highest at solar noon, when it stands due south of you in the Northern Hemisphere and due north in the Southern. How high it climbs depends on your latitude and the season. At the March and September equinoxes the noon sun stands at 90° minus your latitude. At midsummer it is 23.4° higher, and at midwinter 23.4° lower, because that is how far the Earth’s axis is tilted.

blocks.caption: The noon sun at Kansas City (39.1° N) on December 21

blocks.text: A panel faces that sun squarely when it is tilted 90° − 27.5° = 62.5° from flat. In June the same sun stands at 74.3°, and the square-on tilt is under 16°. A fixed panel can’t follow that swing, so its best angle for the year is a compromise between the two.

sections.title: Direction: face the equator

blocks.text: Point the front of the panel toward the equator. In the US, Canada, Europe and most of Asia that means south; in Australia, New Zealand, southern Africa and most of South America, north. Facing the equator puts the panel square to the sun around midday, when the sunlight is strongest.

Direction matters more than tilt, but small errors cost little. In Kansas City, turning the panel 45° away from due south, to face southeast or southwest, costs 6% to 8% of a year’s output. Facing due east or west costs a fifth to a quarter. Facing away from the equator costs about half, and more the steeper the panel.

blocks.caption: Share of the best yearly output at Kansas City (39.1° N), by tilt and direction
blocks.note: Modeled with PVGIS from 2005–2023 weather, for a fixed panel with 14% system losses. Facing east did slightly better than west here: 80% against 78% at 30°.

blocks.text: True north and the compass

The direction to face is true south, or true north below the equator: the line toward the geographic pole, as on a map. A magnetic compass points to the magnetic pole instead, and the angle between the two, called declination, depends on where you are. Magnetic north is about 15° east of true north in Seattle and 14° west of it in Boston, so a compass held on 180° there leaves a panel 15° or 14° off true south.

The planner shows what a compass should read at your spot. Many phone compass apps can show true north instead; look for the setting. Either way, precision isn’t needed: in Kansas City, a panel 15° off due south lost about 1% of a year’s output.

Close to the magnetic poles, in the Canadian Arctic and parts of Antarctica, a compass may be well off or useless. There, line the panel up with the sun at solar noon, when it stands due south, or due north below the equator.
When the best direction isn’t free

On a roof, the roof decides. A slope facing southeast or southwest is nearly as good as one facing south. An east or west slope still collects three-quarters or more at a moderate pitch, and on a flat roof the direction stops mattering. If due south puts the panel in a tree’s afternoon shadow while southeast keeps it clear, take the clear sun: the turn costs well under a tenth, and shade can cost a third or more while it lasts.

sections.title: Tilt: a little less than your latitude

blocks.text: For a panel fixed at one angle all year, the best tilt is close to your latitude, and usually a few degrees less. Geometry alone would say equal to the latitude, but two things pull it lower. Clouds scatter light across the whole sky, and a flatter panel sees more of the sky. And summer days are longer, so an angle that favors the high summer sun collects more over a year.

The planner uses the curves Jacobson and Jadhav fitted in 2018 to the best fixed angles for every country in the world. Checked against PVGIS, the European Commission’s solar model built on satellite and weather records, the fitted angle collected 98.9% to 100% of the best possible at all eight places we tried.

blocks.caption: The all-year tilt, and what lying flat costs
blocks.note: The tilt is the planner’s figure, facing the equator; Singapore’s is raised to the 10° minimum. The last column is a flat panel’s yearly output as a share of the best angle’s, from PVGIS with 2005–2023 weather.

blocks.text: The farther from the equator, the more a tilt is worth. Near the equator a flat panel gives up almost nothing; at Kansas City it gives up a sixth, and at Anchorage more than a quarter.
Close enough is fine

Near the best angle, the output barely changes. In Kansas City, 30° and 45° each collected 99% of what the best angle, 37°, did. Use the nearest notch on a bracket, or the pitch of the roof, if it is within about 10° of the planner’s figure. If you get snow, err on the steep side.

Keep at least 10° of tilt anywhere. Rain then runs off and rinses the glass, where a flatter panel holds puddles that dry into dirt. Near the equator, where the best angle is almost flat, 10° costs about 1%.

sections.title: Changing the angle with the seasons

blocks.text: A mount you can adjust lets the panel follow the sun’s height through the year: steeper in winter, flatter in summer. In Kansas City, changing the angle twice a year, to 15° from April to September and 55° from October to March, collected 4.7% more than the best fixed angle. Changing it every month added 5.9%.

blocks.caption: The best angle for each month at Kansas City (39.1° N)
blocks.note: From PVGIS with 2005–2023 weather, facing south, to the nearest of the angles tried: flat, 15°, 20°, 25°, 30°, 37°, 45°, 50°, 55°, 60°, 65°, 70° and 90°.

blocks.text: Two things stand out. Summer wants a flatter panel than the noon sun suggests: in June and July the sun rises in the northeast and sets in the northwest, and a flat panel catches the morning and evening light that a south-facing tilt turns its back on. And winter rewards a steep angle, which also sheds snow sooner. The planner’s month view shows the noon sun and the sunrise and sunset directions for any month where you are.

sections.title: Portable panels: follow the sun

blocks.text: A folding panel on its stand can beat any fixed mount, because you can move it. Most of the gain comes from turning it to face the sun’s direction a few times a day. Jacobson and Jadhav found that a panel turned to follow the sun around the horizon, at a fixed tilt, collects within 1% to 3% of one that tracks the sun exactly, which worldwide averages 17% more than the best fixed angle.

items: **In the morning,** face the panel toward the sun, roughly where the planner’s sunrise line points, and tilt it steeply, because the morning sun is low.
**Around midday,** turn it toward the equator and set the tilt to the planner’s noon figure for the month.
**In the afternoon,** turn it toward the sunset side and steepen it again as the sun drops.
**Each time,** check the aim: stand a pen upright on the panel. When the pen casts no shadow, the panel faces the sun squarely.

blocks.text: Three moves a day is plenty. Within 25° of square a panel still catches 90% of the direct beam, so an aim that drifts for an hour or two costs little. The hours either side of noon carry most of a day’s energy, so put the panel out by mid-morning.

Turning pays most far from the equator in summer. There the sun rises in the northeast and sets in the northwest (southeast and southwest below the equator), behind a panel that faces the equator, and only a panel you can turn catches that light.

sections.title: Where to put it: shade first

blocks.text: Shade costs more than any angle. A shadow over part of a panel holds back the cells wired to it, so a patch the size of a hand can take a third or more of the output while it lasts. Before you mount anything, watch the spot through a sunny day, and think about the season: the sun is lowest in winter, so shadows are longest then.

The planner’s noon-shadow figure says how far shadows reach when the sun is highest. In Kansas City, a post’s noon shadow in late December is almost twice the post’s height; in June it is about a quarter. So a 6 ft fence 10 ft from a panel shades it at midday in winter but not in summer.

Shadows swing round with the sun, too. In the morning and evening they stretch away from the east and west, so trees and buildings on those sides matter for those hours, and anything tall on the equator side matters all day. Panels in rows shade each other the same way when the sun is low: space the rows by at least the winter noon shadow of the row in front.

sections.title: Mounting: air, cable and wind

blocks.text: A panel loses about 0.3% to 0.5% of its power for every degree Celsius its cells warm above 25 °C (77 °F), so let air reach its back. On a roof, a gap of a few inches under the panel keeps it cooler than one laid on the shingles. On the ground, stand a portable panel on its legs rather than on hot rock, sand or a car roof.

Keep the cable from the panel to the power station short. Use the panel’s own lead where you can, and a short, thick extension where you can’t: a long, thin one wastes power as heat. If you wire panels in series, check their total voltage against the power station’s input limit for the coldest morning you expect, as the [charging guide](/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station#solar-panel-charging-power-station-matching-panels) explains.
A tilted panel catches wind like a sail. Weigh down or stake a portable panel’s stand, fold it away before a storm, and on a roof or an RV follow the mount maker’s limits for tilt and wind.

sections.title: Snow, dust and rain

blocks.text: Snow on the glass blocks the light almost completely, and a steeper panel sheds it sooner. Where snow is common, set a fixed panel toward the steep end of its range: in Kansas City, going 8° steeper than the best angle cost under 1% of a year’s output. Clear a buried panel with a soft brush, never a scraper.
Dust, pollen and bird droppings build up fastest on flat panels. At 10° or more, rain does most of the cleaning; in a dry spell, rinse the glass with water and a soft cloth.

articles.title: How to Choose the Best Power Station for Camping
articles.summary: The best power station for camping is the smallest one that keeps your fridge, lights and devices going until you can recharge it. This guide shows how to size one for your trip, and what to check for weight, solar, cold, rain and campground rules.
articles.imageAlt: A camper in a hooded sweatshirt sits in a folding chair with a mug next to a yellow tent and a wheeled power station, with snow-capped mountains and an orange expedition truck behind them.

sections.title: The short answer

blocks.text: For a weekend of car camping with a 12 V fridge, lights and phones, look for about 1,500 Wh of capacity. One night of CPAP takes about 500 Wh. For a week or more, a battery big enough to last on its own gets too heavy to carry, so pair a unit of about 750 Wh with 200 W of solar panel instead.

Then check four things. The fridge and gadgets should run from the 12 V and USB-C ports, so no power is wasted in the inverter. You should be able to carry it, which for most people means about 30 lb or less. Its solar input should fit the panels you plan to bring. And the battery should be lithium iron phosphate (LFP), which lasts thousands of cycles.

blocks.caption: What common camping trips need
rows: A remote workday at camp, 24 hours
Laptop, Starlink Mini, phone, 12 V fridge, lights
blocks.note: Worked with the calculator’s default devices in mild weather, with losses and a 20% reserve included. Every trip but the last runs on one full charge. The last counts on average sun to refill the battery each day.

blocks.text: [The calculator](/calculator/use-case) works this out for your own gear: choose Outdoor, add your devices and say how long the trip lasts.

sections.title: What size power station do you need for camping?

blocks.text: The size comes from what you plug in and how long it has to last before you can recharge it. Three steps get you there:

items: **List your gear and its watts.** The figure is on the label or the charger. A 12 V fridge, a CPAP, lights and phones cover most camping trips.
**Work out a day of use.** Multiply each device’s watts by the hours it runs. For a fridge, count only the share of the day its compressor actually runs.
**Multiply by the days until you recharge, then by 1.5.** The extra half covers what is lost on the way out of the battery and keeps a reserve in it.

blocks.caption: A day of camping gear
blocks.note: These are the values the calculator starts from. Your own devices may use more or less, so check their labels.

blocks.caption: A weekend with a 12 V fridge, lights and a phone

rows.label: Energy the devices use in a day
Losses and reserve, as a quick rule

blocks.text: The calculator’s full sum for the same weekend comes to 1,455 Wh, so a unit of about 1,500 Wh is the right size. The [buying guide](/guides/how-to-choose-portable-power-station#how-to-choose-portable-power-station-capacity) walks through every step of that sum.

Watts matter less at camp than at home. Almost nothing on a camping list draws much, so even a small unit’s output covers it. The exceptions are the things that make heat: a kettle, a coffee maker, a hair dryer or an electric cooktop. Those decide the size of the inverter, as the section on cooking shows.

sections.title: How long will a power station run a 12 V fridge?

blocks.text: A compressor fridge is the biggest steady load on most camping trips, and the main reason campers outgrow a power bank. Its compressor draws about 45 W while it runs, but it runs only part of the time, more on a hot day and less on a cool one.
Makers rate these fridges by average current. Dometic gives its CFX3 45 as 1.03 Ah per hour at 90 °F outside with 39 °F inside, which comes to about 300 Wh a day at 12 V.

blocks.caption: A Dometic CFX3 45 on a hot day, by its maker’s figure

blocks.text: The calculator counts more, 432 Wh a day, with the compressor running 40% of the time. That leaves room for a fridge filled with warm drinks, a lid that opens often and a car that heats up in the sun.

blocks.caption: Days a 12 V fridge runs on one charge
blocks.note: A 45 W fridge running 40% of the day, with 95% of the rated capacity usable and the battery run down to empty. Through an AC outlet, the inverter loses about 8% and draws 5 W of its own around the clock.

blocks.text: Plug the fridge into the 12 V socket, not an AC outlet. Through the inverter it loses more power and keeps the inverter switched on all day: for one day of fridge alone, the calculator asks for 590 Wh of capacity on 12 V and 750 Wh on AC.

items: Chill the fridge and everything in it at home on wall power the night before. Cooling warm food and drinks is the hardest work it does.
Keep it in the shade with room around its vents, and open it less often.
Keep it at 40 °F or a little below, the limit for food safety, but no colder than you need.

A thermoelectric cooler, the cheaper kind without a compressor, runs nonstop instead of cycling and can only cool so far below the outside air. On a battery it seldom saves energy, and it keeps food less cold.

sections.title: Can a power station run a CPAP while camping?

blocks.text: Yes, and it is one of the most common reasons campers buy one. The calculator counts a CPAP at 40 W for 8 hours, 320 Wh a night. With losses and a reserve, one night calls for about 490 Wh through an AC outlet and 440 Wh on a 12 V cable. Three nights call for about 1,500 Wh and 1,350 Wh.

items: **Use a DC cable if your machine has one.** ResMed sells a DC converter for its AirSense 10 and 11 that runs the machine from a 12 V or 24 V source, which skips the inverter and its losses.
**The humidifier and heated tube are the big draw.** ResMed’s own battery run times don’t apply when they are in use. Ask your doctor before you change your settings to save power.
**Test a full night at home first,** on the power station, with the settings you will use at camp. The display shows what the machine really draws.
**Keep enough for a second night,** in case the next day is cloudy or you can’t recharge.

sections.title: Can you cook, boil water or heat a tent with a power station?

blocks.text: You can, but heat is the most expensive thing to ask of a battery. A kettle, coffee maker or cooktop draws 900 to 1,800 W, so it sets the size of the inverter as well as using up capacity.

blocks.caption: Heating appliances at camp
rows: About 120 Wh to boil a liter
900 Wh for 30 minutes at full power
1,500 Wh for an hour at full power
blocks.note: Output with the calculator’s margins: 10% on top for short use, 25% for a heater that runs for hours. From the battery, add about 8% for the inverter.

blocks.text: Boiling a liter of cold water takes about 120 Wh, roughly five minutes at 1,500 W, so a 1,500 Wh power station can make coffee or tea every morning of a weekend, if its inverter is big enough. Cooking whole meals is another matter. A camp stove does that better, outdoors, and leaves the battery for the fridge.

Heating a tent doesn’t work on a battery. At full power a space heater empties 1,000 Wh in about 35 minutes. Rely on your sleeping bag and warm clothes instead. A heated blanket or pad, which uses tens of watts instead of a heater’s 1,500 W, is the one kind of electric heat that makes sense on a power station.

Never run a fuel-burning stove, heater, lantern or generator inside a tent or camper, even with the door open. They give off carbon monoxide, which is most dangerous to people asleep. A power station burns no fuel and is safe inside the tent.

sections.title: How to recharge a power station while camping

blocks.text: How you recharge decides the size more than anything else. A week of a 12 V fridge, lights and a phone on one charge takes about 5,100 Wh, a unit of well over 100 lb. With 200 W of solar panel in average sun, a unit of about 730 Wh does the same job, because the panel refills each day what the battery gave.
Solar panels

A portable panel puts about three times its rated watts into the battery on an average day, counted in watt-hours: 630 Wh from a 200 W panel, about 350 Wh in limited sun, and a quarter of a typical day under heavy cloud. For the fridge, lights and phone above, about 200 W of panel keeps up in average sun and about 350 W in limited sun.

Many campsites sit under trees, and shade costs a panel far more than its size suggests. Put the panel in the sunniest open spot you can reach, and turn it to follow the sun two or three times a day. The [guide to aiming a panel](/guides/solar-panel-direction-and-tilt#solar-panel-direction-and-tilt-portable) shows how.

Before you buy panels, check the power station’s solar input: its maximum watts, the voltage range it accepts and its connector. The [solar charging guide](/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station#solar-panel-charging-power-station-matching-panels) shows how to match them.
The car

A 12 V socket gives about 100 W, so a four-hour drive puts back at most about 400 Wh: enough to top up a small unit, not to refill a large one. Alternator chargers, wired to the car’s battery, deliver 500 to 800 W while the engine runs.

An electric car with a household outlet, often called vehicle-to-load or V2L, charges a power station as a wall outlet would. The calculator lists the cars whose makers confirm such an outlet and checks each power station against it.
Campground power
At a site with an electric hookup, plug the power station’s charger into the pedestal’s regular 120 V outlet and recharge as you would at home. Many current units refill 1,000 Wh in about an hour.
A generator

Where generators are allowed, an hour or two a day refills a power station, and the battery carries the quiet hours. Parks limit when they may run: Yosemite allows generators only from 7 to 9 a.m., noon to 2 p.m. and 5 to 7 p.m. Use an inverter generator, since most power stations need clean power to charge.

sections.title: How heavy a power station can you carry?

blocks.text: Weight comes with capacity: current LFP units weigh 20 to 30 lb for every 1,000 Wh. So decide first how far you will carry it.

blocks.caption: Weight, and what each size covers at camp
rows: Lights, phones and a camera for a night or two
Two nights of CPAP, or a week of 12 V fridge, lights and phone with 200 W of solar
A weekend of 12 V fridge, lights and phone
A long weekend, or a weekend with a CPAP
blocks.note: Weights of LFP models on sale in 2026, from makers’ specifications. What each size covers uses the calculator’s default devices in mild weather.

blocks.text: About 30 lb is comfortable to carry in one hand from the car to the campsite. Above that, look for wheels and a pull handle, or plan on a cart for walk-in sites. If you camp from the car or an RV and the unit stays put, weight matters much less.

For backpacking, leave the power station at home. A 20,000 mAh power bank stores about 74 Wh, enough for several phone charges, and fits in a pocket. It is also the only kind of battery you can fly with: airline rules cap lithium-ion batteries at 100 Wh, or 160 Wh with the airline’s approval.

sections.title: Which ports matter at camp

items: **A 12 V car socket** for the fridge. Most give up to about 120 W, plenty for a fridge, a tire inflator or a 12 V heated blanket. If a CPAP will also run on 12 V, count the 12 V outputs.
**USB-C ports of 60 to 100 W** for phones, laptops, cameras and lights. A Starlink Mini can run from USB-C too, but only from a port that delivers 100 W, and with Starlink’s own USB-C cable.
**AC outlets** only for what needs them: a drone or e-bike charger, a projector, a coffee maker. Switch them off when nothing is plugged in, since the inverter uses power just by being on.
**A screen that shows watts in and out** and the time left. At camp it is the only way to know whether the solar panel is keeping up.

sections.title: Cold, heat, rain and dust

blocks.text: Cold

A battery gives back less in the cold: about 90% of its rated capacity between 32 and 50 °F, and about 80% below freezing. Most LFP units also refuse to charge below 32 °F, so on a frosty morning the solar panel does nothing until the battery warms up. For a weekend with the fridge, lights and phone, the calculator asks for 1,500 Wh in mild weather, 1,650 Wh in cool weather and 1,850 Wh below freezing.

At night, keep the power station in the tent or the car, off the cold ground. If you camp in real cold, sodium-ion units charge down to 5 °F and run down to −13 °F, at the cost of extra weight. The [buying guide](/guides/how-to-choose-portable-power-station#how-to-choose-portable-power-station-battery) compares the battery types.
Heat

Most units are rated to run up to about 104 to 113 °F. A closed car in summer sun gets far hotter than that, so don’t leave the power station in one. At camp, keep the unit in the shade and let only the panel sit in the sun.
Rain, sand and dust

Most power stations have no protection against water or dust. Keep yours under the vestibule, an awning or the tailgate, off wet ground and out of blowing sand. A few camping models carry an IP65 rating, which means dust-tight and protected against low-pressure jets of water. Even those aren’t meant to sit out in the rain or in a puddle.

sections.title: Noise and campground rules

blocks.text: A power station is silent except for its fans, which spin up when it charges fast or runs a heavy load. If it charges overnight next to your tent, set a slow charging speed in the app.

Generators are a different story. National parks forbid generators louder than 60 dB, measured at 50 feet, and campgrounds set hours for the quiet ones. In Yosemite that means three two-hour windows a day, and never during quiet hours from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Some campgrounds keep separate loops for sites that run generators.

Those rules are written for engines. A power station has no engine noise and no exhaust, so it can keep the fridge and a CPAP running through the night. Each campground can add its own rules, so read them before you go.

sections.title: What else to check

items: **Battery type.** LFP lasts 3,000 cycles or more and is now standard. A lighter NMC unit can still make sense if you carry it on foot and use it a few times a year.
**Solar input.** Enough watts for the panels you plan to carry, a voltage range that fits them, and a connector you have a cable for.
**Wall charging speed.** A fast charger lets you top up at home the morning you leave, or at a campground outlet in an hour or two.
**Pass-through charging.** Running the fridge while the panel charges the battery is how a camp setup normally works, and most units do it.
**Safety and warranty.** A UL 2743 listing, no open recall, and a warranty of three to five years.
**Price per watt-hour.** Divide the price by the capacity to compare units of different sizes.

blocks.text: The [buying guide](/guides/how-to-choose-portable-power-station) covers each of these in detail.

sections.title: Before you go

items: Charge it full at home, and chill the fridge on wall power the night before.
Run your real setup for a night at home: the fridge, the CPAP, the lights. The display tells you what a night actually costs.
Pack the cables: the 12 V cord for the fridge, the CPAP’s DC cable, the panel’s adapter cable and the AC charger.
Plan where everything goes at camp: the panel in the sun, the power station in the shade and out of the rain.

sections.title: A camping checklist before you buy

items: **Capacity** covers your gear until you can recharge, with about half again on top: about 1,500 Wh for a weekend with a 12 V fridge, about 500 Wh for a night of CPAP.
**Recharging** is planned: solar watts and voltage that fit the input, or a way to charge from the car or a campground outlet.
**A 12 V socket and USB-C ports** cover the fridge and electronics, so the inverter can stay off.
**Output** covers the largest heating appliance you will bring, or that appliance stays at home.
**Weight** is about 30 lb or less if you will carry it, or the unit has wheels.
**The battery** is LFP, and you have a plan for cold nights: the unit sleeps in the tent or the car.
**Shelter** is ready: somewhere dry to put it, or an IP rating if it has to sit outside.
**Safety** is covered: a UL 2743 listing, no open recall, and a warranty of three to five years.
